absorption spectrum: A pattern of dark lines formed when electrons absorb specific photon energies from continuous light.
abundance: The relative proportion, usually a percentage, in which an isotope occurs in nature.
alpha particle: A positively charged helium nucleus of two protons and two neutrons.
angular momentum quantum number, l: A quantum number that determines an orbital's shape (s=0, p=1, d=2, f=3).
atomic mass unit, amu: A unit of mass defined as one-twelfth the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
atomic number, z: The number of protons in an atom, which identifies the element.
atomic radius: A measure of atom size reflecting how tightly the nucleus holds outer electrons.
aufbau principle: The rule that electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals available first.
average atomic mass: The weighted average mass of an element's naturally occurring isotopes.
bohr model: A model in which electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed circular paths.
density: The mass of a substance per unit of its volume.
diagonal rule: A diagram-based rule giving the order in which orbitals fill with electrons.
effective nuclear charge, z_eff: The net positive pull an outer electron actually feels after shielding.
effective nuclear charge, zeff: The net nuclear charge an outer electron feels after subtracting shielding.
electromagnetic spectrum: The full range of light by wavelength and frequency, from radio waves to gamma rays.
electron: A negatively charged particle outside the nucleus that governs chemical reactions.
electron pair repulsion: The repulsion between two paired electrons sharing one orbital.
electronegativity: A relative measure of an atom's ability to attract shared bonding electrons.
electrostatic repulsion: The repulsive force between like charges.
emission spectrum: The bright lines emitted as excited electrons fall to lower energy levels.
energy level: A discrete, allowed energy value that an electron can have.
excited state: A state in which an electron has absorbed energy and moved to a higher level.
fractional abundance: The fraction, as a decimal, of an element's atoms that are a given isotope.
frequency, f: The number of wave cycles per second, measured in hertz.
frequency, ν: The number of oscillations per second, proportional to photon energy.
gold foil experiment: Rutherford's alpha-scattering experiment providing evidence for the nuclear model.
ground state: The state in which an atom's electrons occupy the lowest possible energy.
half-filled subshell: An especially stable arrangement with one electron in each orbital of a subshell.
hund's rule: The rule that electrons occupy equal-energy orbitals singly before pairing.
ionization energy: The energy needed to remove the most loosely held electron from a gaseous atom.
isotope: Atoms of an element with the same protons but different numbers of neutrons.
isotope notation: A way of writing an isotope that shows its mass number, such as carbon-14.
isotopes: Atoms of the same element with the same protons but differing neutron numbers.
line spectrum: A discrete set of wavelengths unique to an element, serving as its fingerprint.
magnetic quantum number, ml: A quantum number giving the spatial orientation of an orbital, from −l to +l.
mass number, a: The total count of protons and neutrons in an atom's nucleus.
mass spectrometry: A technique that separates ions by mass-to-charge ratio to measure isotopes.
mass-to-charge ratio, m/z: The ratio by which a mass spectrometer separates ions.
neutron: An uncharged particle in the nucleus that distinguishes one isotope from another.
nuclear model: Rutherford's model of a dense central nucleus surrounded by orbiting electrons.
nucleus: The small, dense, positively charged center of an atom holding nearly all its mass.
nuclide: A specific type of atom defined by its number of protons and neutrons.
orbital: A region of space where an electron is most likely found, holding up to two electrons.
pauli exclusion principle: The rule that no two electrons in an atom can share all four quantum numbers.
photoelectric effect: The release of electrons from a metal struck by light above a threshold frequency.
photon: A discrete quantum of light energy, equal to E = hf.
planck's constant, h: The constant 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s linking a photon's energy to its frequency.
plum pudding model: Thomson's model of electrons embedded in a spread-out positive charge.
plum-pudding model: Thomson's earlier model of electrons embedded in a positive pudding, later disproved.
principal quantum number, n: A quantum number giving an electron's energy level and orbital size.
probability cloud: A visual representation of an orbital, denser where electrons are more likely.
proton: A positively charged particle in the nucleus whose count defines the element.
quantized energy levels: The discrete, stepped energy values allowed for electrons in an atom.
quantum mechanical model: The modern model describing electrons as probability distributions in orbitals.
shielding: The reduction of nuclear attraction on outer electrons by inner-shell electrons.
spin quantum number, ms: A quantum number giving an electron's spin as +½ or −½.
threshold frequency: The minimum light frequency needed to eject an electron from a metal.
uncertainty principle: Heisenberg's principle that position and momentum cannot both be known exactly.
valence electrons: The outermost-shell electrons that determine an atom's chemical behavior.
wavelength, λ: The length of one cycle of a wave, inversely related to its energy.
weighted average atomic mass: The average isotope mass of an element weighted by each isotope's abundance.
alloy: A mixture of a metal with other elements that increases hardness.
anion: A negatively charged ion formed when an atom gains electrons.
anomalous property: An unexpected property of water, such as its high boiling point.
bent: A molecular shape that is bent due to lone pairs, as in water.
bent, angular: A bent shape from two bonds and two lone pairs, as in water (~104.5°).
boiling point: The temperature at which a liquid's vapor pressure equals atmospheric pressure.
bond angle: The angle between two bonds meeting at a central atom.
bond order: The number of shared electron pairs between two bonded atoms.
bond polarity: The degree of partial charge in a bond from an electronegativity difference.
bonding pair: A shared pair of electrons forming a covalent bond.
brittleness: The tendency of an ionic solid to shatter when its layers shift and repel.
cation: A positively charged ion formed when an atom loses electrons.
charge carrier: A particle that carries electric current, such as electrons or ions.
coulomb's law: The law that electrostatic force is proportional to charges and inversely to distance squared.
covalent bond: A bond formed by sharing one or more electron pairs between nonmetal atoms.
crystal lattice: The regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of ions in a solid.
delocalization: The spreading of electrons over several atoms rather than one bond.
delocalized electron: An electron free to move throughout a metal rather than fixed to one atom.
delocalized electrons: Valence electrons that move freely throughout a metal, not bound to one atom.
dipole: A separation of partial positive and negative charge across a bond or molecule.
dipole moment: A vector quantity giving the size and direction of charge separation.
dipole-dipole force: The attraction between the permanent dipoles of polar molecules.
ductility: The ability of a metal to be drawn into wires without breaking.
electrical conductivity: The ability to carry electric charge, requiring free charge carriers.
electron domain: A group of bonding or nonbonding electrons around a central atom.
electron domain geometry: The arrangement of all electron domains, including lone pairs.
electron geometry: The arrangement of all electron groups, bonds and lone pairs, around an atom.
electron group: A bond of any order or a lone pair around a central atom, counted as one.
electron sea model: A model of metal cations immersed in a sea of free electrons.
electron-deficient: A stable molecule with fewer than eight electrons around the central atom.
electron-sea model: A picture of metal as cations bathed in a sea of delocalized electrons.
electronegativity difference: The difference in electronegativity between two atoms, setting bond polarity.
expanded octet: More than eight valence electrons around a central atom, as in SF₆.
formal charge: A bookkeeping charge used to choose the best Lewis structure.
hydrogen bond: A strong dipole attraction when hydrogen is bonded to N, O, or F.
hydrogen bonding: An especially strong intermolecular attraction when H is bonded to N, O, or F.
intermolecular force, imf: An attractive force between molecules that governs changes of state.
intramolecular bond: A bond holding atoms within a molecule, stronger than intermolecular forces.
ionic bond: The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions formed by electron transfer.
ionic crystal: A solid lattice of regularly arranged positive and negative ions.
ionic radius: The size of an ion; smaller ions give shorter, stronger ionic bonds.
lattice energy: The energy released when gaseous ions form one mole of a solid ionic lattice.
lewis dot structure: A diagram showing an atom's bonding and nonbonding electrons as dots and lines.
lewis structure: A diagram showing bonding pairs and lone pairs for all atoms in a molecule.
london dispersion force: An attraction from temporary induced dipoles, present in all molecules.
london dispersion force, ldf: A weak force from instantaneous dipoles, present in all molecules.
lone pair: A valence electron pair localized on one atom and not used in bonding.
lone pair repulsion: The strong repulsion of lone pairs that narrows bond angles.
luster: The shine of a metal caused by delocalized electrons reflecting light.
malleability: The ability of a metal to be hammered into sheets as its layers slide.
melting point: The temperature at which a solid becomes a liquid.
metallic bond: The attraction between metal cations and a surrounding sea of delocalized electrons.
molecular geometry: The shape of a molecule defined by atom positions, ignoring lone pairs.
molecular polarity: Whether a molecule has a net dipole, set by the vector sum of bond dipoles.
molecular symmetry: A geometric balance in which bond dipoles cancel to give a nonpolar molecule.
net dipole: The overall molecular dipole remaining after vector addition.
net dipole moment: The overall direction and magnitude of charge separation in a molecule.
nonpolar molecule: A molecule whose net dipole is zero.
octet rule: The tendency of atoms to gain, lose, or share electrons to reach eight valence electrons.
partial charge, δ: A fractional charge from unequal electron sharing, not a full ionic charge.
polar covalent bond: A covalent bond in which electrons are shared unequally.
polarizability: How easily an electron cloud distorts; greater polarizability means stronger dispersion forces.
resonance hybrid: The actual structure of a molecule, an average of its resonance structures.
resonance structure: One of several valid Lewis structures representing the same molecule.
surface tension: A film-like effect at a liquid's surface caused by cohesive intermolecular forces.
symmetry: A balanced arrangement of bonds that causes dipoles to cancel.
thermal conductivity: The ability to transfer heat, rapid in metals due to free electrons.
trigonal pyramidal: A shape from three bonds and one lone pair, as in NH₃ (~107°).
vector addition: The operation of adding dipoles by direction and magnitude.
volatility: How readily a substance evaporates; higher when intermolecular forces are weak.
vsepr theory: The theory that electron groups arrange themselves to minimize repulsion.
δen: The difference in electron-attracting power between two bonded atoms.
100 g assumption: A shortcut of assuming 100 g of a compound so each percent equals that many grams.
actual yield: The amount of product actually obtained in an experiment.
amount of substance: The quantity of particles, measured in moles.
amount remaining: The moles of excess reactant left after the limiting reactant is used up.
atomic mass: The weighted average mass of an element's isotopes in atomic mass units.
avogadro's number: The number of particles in one mole, 6.022 × 10²³.
balancing by inspection: Adjusting coefficients by trial and error to equalize atoms on both sides.
carbon-12 standard: The standard defining one mole as the atoms in 12 g of carbon-12.
chemical equation: A representation of reactants and products using formulas and an arrow.
coefficient: A number before a formula giving the count of formula units in an equation.
conversion factor: A ratio used as a fraction to convert between two units.
dimensional analysis: A method of converting units by multiplying by conversion factors.
driving force: The condition that pushes a reaction forward until a reactant runs out.
elemental analysis: An experimental method measuring the mass proportion of each element in a compound.
empirical formula: A formula showing the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound.
empirical formula mass: The molar mass of one empirical formula unit.
excess reactant: A reactant that remains after the limiting reactant is consumed.
formula mass: The sum of the atomic masses of all atoms in one formula unit.
initial moles: The number of moles of a reactant present before a reaction begins.
integer multiplier n: The whole number satisfying molecular formula = n × empirical formula.
law of conservation of mass: The law that mass is conserved in a chemical reaction; atoms are neither created nor destroyed.
limiting reactant: The reactant consumed first that stops the reaction and sets the maximum product.
mass-to-mass stoichiometry: Calculating product mass from reactant mass via mass-mole-mole-mass steps.
molar mass: The mass of one mole of a substance, in grams per mole.
mole: The unit of amount equal to 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
mole ratio: The ratio of moles between substances given by balanced equation coefficients.
mole ratio reduction: Dividing mole values by the smallest to get the simplest whole-number ratio.
mole, mol: The SI base unit of amount, equal to 6.022 × 10²³ particles.
molecular formula: A formula giving the actual number of atoms in one molecule.
moles consumed: The moles that actually take part in a reaction, found from the limiting reactant.
percent composition: The mass percentage of each element in a compound.
percent yield: Actual yield divided by theoretical yield times 100 percent.
polyatomic ion: A group of atoms bonded together that carries an overall charge, such as sulfate.
product: A substance formed by a reaction, written to the right of the arrow.
reactant: A starting substance in a reaction, written to the left of the arrow.
stoichiometric ratio: The mole ratio of reactants required by a balanced equation.
stoichiometry: The study of quantitative relationships between reactants and products.
subscript: A number below a symbol giving the count of atoms in a molecule; fixed when balancing.
theoretical yield: The maximum product mass calculated assuming the limiting reactant fully reacts.
bond energy: The energy needed to break one mole of a specific bond in the gas phase.
calorimeter: An insulated device that measures heat exchange from temperature change.
calorimetry: The experimental measurement of heat flow in physical or chemical change.
conservation of energy: The principle that energy is neither created nor destroyed, only transferred.
disorder: The randomness in the arrangement of particles and energy, measured by entropy.
endothermic: Describing a reaction that absorbs heat from its surroundings (ΔH > 0).
endothermic reaction: A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings.
enthalpy of reaction, δh: The heat absorbed or released by a reaction at constant pressure.
enthalpy, h: The heat content of a system at constant pressure, tracked by its change ΔH.
entropy, s: A measure of a system's disorder or number of accessible microstates.
exothermic: Describing a reaction that releases heat to its surroundings (ΔH < 0).
exothermic reaction: A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings.
gibbs free energy, g: A thermodynamic quantity whose change predicts spontaneity: ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
gibbs free energy, δg: The quantity determining spontaneity, equal to ΔH − TΔS.
heat capacity: The heat required to raise an entire sample's temperature by one degree.
heat of fusion, l_f: The energy to convert one gram or mole of solid to liquid at the melting point.
heat of fusion, δh_fus: The heat required for the solid-to-liquid phase change.
heat of vaporization, l_v: The energy to convert one gram or mole of liquid to gas at the boiling point.
heat of vaporization, δh_vap: The heat required for the liquid-to-gas phase change.
heat, q: Thermal energy flowing from a hotter to a colder object.
heating curve: A graph of temperature versus added energy showing sloped phases and flat phase changes.
hess's law: The law that a reaction's total ΔH equals the sum of the ΔH values of its steps.
intermolecular forces: Attractions between molecules that must be overcome during phase changes.
kelvin, k: The unit of absolute temperature, required for ΔG calculations.
kinetic energy: The energy of particle motion, measured by temperature.
latent heat: Energy absorbed or released during a phase change at constant temperature.
overcoming imf: The work of breaking intermolecular forces to separate molecules during a phase change.
phase change: A transition between solid, liquid, and gas at constant temperature.
plateau: A flat region of a heating curve where temperature stays constant during a phase change.
second law of thermodynamics: The law that the total entropy of the universe increases in a spontaneous process.
specific heat capacity: The heat needed to raise one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius.
specific heat capacity, c: The energy needed to raise one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius.
spontaneity: Whether a process can occur on its own, determined by the sign of ΔG.
spontaneous process: A change that proceeds on its own without continuous outside energy.
spontaneous reaction: A reaction that proceeds without outside intervention (ΔG < 0).
standard enthalpy of formation, δhf°: The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements.
standard state: The reference condition of 1 bar and usually 25 °C.
state function: A property depending only on the present state, not the path, such as enthalpy.
sublimation: The phase change from solid directly to gas without passing through liquid.
temperature: A measure of the average kinetic energy of particles in a substance.
temperature-dependent spontaneity: A case where the sign of ΔG, and thus spontaneity, changes with temperature.
thermal equilibrium: The state in which two contacting objects reach the same temperature.
δg = 0: The point of equilibrium where forward and reverse drives balance and no net change occurs.
δh°f: The enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from standard-state elements.
5% rule: A check on the small-x approximation: valid if x divided by initial acid times 100 percent is 5 percent or less.
acid dissociation constant, ka: The equilibrium constant for a weak acid's ionization; larger means stronger.
activation energy, ea: The minimum energy colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur.
activity: The effective thermodynamic concentration, taken as 1 for pure solids and liquids.
alternative pathway: A lower-activation-energy reaction route provided by a catalyst.
autoionization: The self-ionization of water into H⁺ and OH⁻, establishing Kw.
base dissociation constant, kb: The equilibrium constant for a weak base's ionization.
catalyst: A substance that lowers activation energy and speeds a reaction without being consumed.
collision theory: The theory that reactions occur from collisions with enough energy and proper orientation.
dynamic equilibrium: A state where forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates.
energy diagram: A graph of potential energy versus reaction progress showing Ea and ΔH.
equilibrium constant, keq: The ratio of product to reactant concentrations at equilibrium, depending only on temperature.
equilibrium shift: The net direction a reaction proceeds to reach a new equilibrium after disturbance.
forward reaction: The reaction proceeding from reactants to products as written.
half-life: The time for a concentration to fall to half its value.
half-life, t₁/₂: The time for reactant concentration to drop to half its current value.
ice table: A table organizing initial, change, and equilibrium concentrations for calculations.
initial rate: The reaction rate just as the reaction begins, when concentrations are near their start.
integrated rate law: An equation giving concentration as a function of time.
kw: The ion-product constant for water, equal to 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 25 °C.
le chatelier's principle: The principle that a stressed equilibrium shifts to partly relieve the stress.
method of initial rates: An experimental method varying one reactant at a time to find each reaction order.
orientation: The spatial alignment of colliding particles needed for a reaction.
ph: The negative logarithm of hydrogen ion concentration; lower means more acidic.
poh: The negative logarithm of hydroxide ion concentration.
pure solid/liquid: A pure phase of fixed molar density, excluded from the equilibrium expression.
rate constant, k: The proportionality constant in a rate law, increasing with temperature.
rate law: An equation giving reaction rate as a function of reactant concentrations.
reaction order: The exponent on a reactant's concentration in the rate law, found experimentally.
reaction quotient, q: An expression like Keq using concentrations at any moment to predict reaction direction.
reaction rate: The amount of reactant consumed or product formed per unit time.
reverse reaction: The reaction proceeding from products back to reactants.
strong acid: An acid that ionizes almost completely in water, such as HCl.
temperature dependence: The property that temperature change alters the value of Keq.
temperature dependence of keq: The change in Keq with temperature as forward and reverse rate constants change unequally.
transition state: The highest-energy, least stable arrangement at the peak of an energy diagram.
weak acid: An acid that only partly ionizes in water, described by Ka.
cell notation: A shorthand representation of a cell as anode | solution || solution | cathode.
cell notation / line notation: A shorthand writing a cell with oxidation on the left and reduction on the right.
cell potential, e°cell: The standard voltage of a cell, equal to E°cathode minus E°anode.
charge neutrality: The condition of no net charge imbalance, maintained by the salt bridge.
coulomb, c: The SI unit of charge, the charge moved by one ampere in one second.
current, i: The rate of charge flow in a circuit, measured in amperes.
electrolysis: Using external electrical energy to drive a nonspontaneous redox reaction.
electrolysis of water: The driven decomposition of water into hydrogen and oxygen gas.
electrolytic cell: A cell in which an external source forces a nonspontaneous reaction.
electroplating: Depositing a thin metal layer onto an object by reduction at the cathode.
extensive property: A property that depends on the amount of matter, such as mass or volume.
external power source: A battery or power supply that provides energy for electrolysis.
faraday constant, f: The charge of one mole of electrons, 96,485 C/mol.
faraday's law: The law that the amount of product at an electrode is proportional to charge passed.
faraday's law of electrolysis: The law relating mass produced at an electrode to the charge passed.
galvanic cell: A cell that produces electricity from a spontaneous redox reaction.
galvanic cell / voltaic cell: A cell converting the energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical work.
half-cell: One compartment of a cell containing an electrode and its solution.
half-reaction: A balanced equation showing only the oxidation or reduction part with electrons.
inert electrolyte: An ionic compound in the salt bridge that does not take part in electrode reactions.
intensive property: A property independent of the amount of matter, such as temperature or density.
metal hydride: A binary metal-hydrogen compound in which hydrogen has an oxidation state of −1.
oxidation: The loss of electrons, raising an atom's oxidation number.
oxidation state/number: A hypothetical charge assigned to an atom to track electron transfer.
oxidizing agent: A reactant that gains electrons and oxidizes another substance.
peroxide: A compound containing O₂²⁻ in which oxygen has an oxidation state of −1.
phase boundary, |: A single bar in cell notation marking the boundary between two phases.
redox reaction: A reaction in which electrons transfer and oxidation numbers change.
reducing agent: A reactant that donates electrons and reduces another substance.
reduction: The gain of electrons, lowering an atom's oxidation number.
salt bridge: A channel of inert electrolyte that lets ions move to keep half-cells neutral.
standard cell potential, e°cell: The voltage of a galvanic cell at standard conditions, E°cathode minus E°anode.
standard hydrogen electrode, she: The reference half-cell defined as E° = 0 V.
standard reduction potential, e°red: The voltage of a reduction half-reaction at standard conditions.
water electrolysis: The use of electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.
δg°: The maximum nonexpansion work a reaction can do at standard conditions, equal to −nFE°cell.
